title: Provably Data-driven Multiple Hyper-parameter Tuning with Structured Loss Function
claim_text: Theorem 4.1 establishes a general first-order-logic framework giving pseudo-dimension bounds of O(p*prod(d_k+1)*log M + p^2*prod(d_k+1)*log Delta) for multi-dimensional hyperparameter tuning by connecting logical complexity to learning-theoretic complexity via quantifier elimination (Section 4). Theorem 5.1 bounds the pseudo-dimension of piecewise-polynomial training-loss objectives (with training loss f equal to validation loss g) as O(p*d*log(M_f+T_f+d) + p^2*d*log Delta_f) for p-dimensional hyperparameters (Section 5). Theorem 6.1 extends the framework to the bi-level validation-loss setting (f not equal to g), establishing Pdim(L) = O(p*d^2*log M_tot + p^2*d^2*log Delta_tot) without requiring identical training and validation objectives (Section 6). title: Positive Distribution Shift as a Framework for Understanding Tractable Learning
claim_text: Noisy parities are D-DS-PAC learnable by an explicit efficient algorithm using m(epsilon) = O(d^2 log^2(d)/epsilon / (1-2eta)^2) samples, despite being conjectured computationally hard under the standard PAC model (Theorem 4.3). Noisy parities are also D-DS-PAC learnable using a stylized layerwise SGD procedure on a 2-layer neural network with L1 regularization and sparsity-dependent initialization (Theorem 4.5). Noisy k-juntas are D-DS-PAC learnable via a Correlational Statistical Query algorithm using O(d^k + 2^k) queries, and are R-DS-PAC learnable via stylized layerwise SGD with a covariance loss using m = O~(d log(1/epsilon) / epsilon^2) samples (Theorems 4.6 and 4.8). title: On Densest $k$-Subgraph Mining and Diagonal Loading: Optimization Landscape and Finite-Step Exact Convergence Analysis
claim_text: Theorem 4 extends the Motzkin-Straus theorem to show the relaxed problem's maximum value equals 1+λ-1/ω, where ω is the largest clique size, establishing that diagonal loading parameter λ≥1 is the minimal value ensuring tightness of the penalty-based relaxation. Corollary 1 proves that when λ≥1 there always exists a global maximizer of the relaxed objective that is integral, so the relaxed and combinatorial problems share the same optimal value. Lemma 1 shows that for λ>1 there does not exist a non-integral local maximizer, establishing the strict dichotomy that all integral stationary points are local maximizers while non-integral stationary points are strict saddles. Theorem 5 shows that increasing the diagonal loading parameter beyond λ=1 introduces additional spurious local maxima, implying λ=1 optimally trades off relaxation tightness against optimization difficulty. title: Convex Distance Operator Transport: A Convex and Geometry-Preserving Formulation
claim_text: CDOT formulates cross-domain distribution alignment as a convex quadratic program over transport polytopes, with Theorem 3.4 establishing existence of an optimal coupling and convexity of the objective (Theorem 3.4). Theorem 3.5 proves the CDOT discrepancy is a valid pseudometric on attributed compact metric-measure spaces, while Theorem 3.7 derives a 'dispersion gap' relating CDOT to Gromov-Wasserstein via ℛ_GW,2(π) − ℛ(π) = 𝒱(π) (Theorem 3.5, Theorem 3.7). On synthetic 2D clustered point clouds with n=500 samples, CDOT achieves a matching MSE of 0.0016±0.00, lower than both FGW (0.0034±0.00) and IsoRank (0.0033±0.00) (Table 2). On the OASIS-3 brain connectome dataset (696 subjects, 170-node networks), CDOT attains 0.6136 matching accuracy under diffusion distance versus 0.1853 for FGW, though FGW outperforms CDOT under geodesic distance (0.5375 vs 0.4640) (Table 3). title: Linear Regression with Unknown Truncation Beyond Gaussian Features
claim_text: The paper gives the first polynomial-time, poly(d/ε), algorithm for truncated linear regression with an unknown survival set under sub-Gaussian (rather than Gaussian) feature distributions (Theorem 3.1). The algorithm assumes a known lower bound α on the truncation/survival probability, sub-Gaussian feature tails, and a well-conditioned observed covariance matrix (Section 3, three main assumptions). Phase I of the algorithm learns the unknown survival set as a union of k intervals via a novel positive-only PAC learning subroutine that runs in poly(k/ε) time (Theorem 3.3). Phase II estimates the regression vector via projected stochastic gradient descent on a perturbed negative log-likelihood objective, after Phase I's set recovery (Section 3). title: Semi-knockoffs: a model-agnostic conditional independence testing method with finite-sample guarantees
claim_text: Semi-knockoffs avoids the train-test data split required by prior conditional-independence testing methods such as HRT while still yielding valid p-values, via nonparametric paired tests requiring only conditional expectations ν_j and ρ_j rather than exact knockoff construction (Theorem 3.3, Section 3.1). Theorem 3.4 establishes that the Semi-knockoffs procedure controls the false discovery rate at level q, i.e. FDR(S_SKO) ≤ q (Theorem 3.4, Section 3.2). Theorem 4.1 shows that for null (non-relevant) features, regularized empirical risk minimizers trained with and without the feature remain close, with an ‖θ̃^j − θ̂‖₂ ≤ O_P(√(log(1/δ)/n)) bound, giving optimization stability guarantees for regularized models (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.2). title: Quantifying the noise sensitivity of the Wasserstein metric for images
claim_text: Theorem 2 bounds the expected signed 1-Wasserstein distance between a clean n-pixel image and its Gaussian-noise-perturbed counterpart by (2/√π)σn log2(n) + (1/(2√π))σn, i.e., growth roughly linear in n with a log factor, for zero-sum noise of standard deviation σ (Theorem 2). Theorem 3 shows that for p-Wasserstein distances with integer p>1, the expected p-th power error is bounded by (4/√π) n σ, so the per-image error scales as (nσ)^(1/p), improving (becoming more noise-robust) as p increases, in contrast to the Euclidean (L2) metric's linear scaling in σ (Theorem 3). Theorems 4 and 5 extend the noise-sensitivity bounds to the deviation between the true and noisy Wasserstein distances computed between two distinct images, rather than a single noisy image against its clean version (Theorems 4-5). title: Bridge Matching Sampler: Scalable Sampling via Generalized Fixed-Point Diffusion Matching
claim_text: Bridge Matching Sampler (BMS) unifies fixed-point diffusion-matching samplers under a single framework based on Nelson's relation and a generalized target score identity, recovering Adjoint Sampling (AS) and Adjoint Schrödinger Bridge Sampler (ASBS) as special cases. Unlike ASBS, which requires alternating optimization, BMS uses independent couplings between prior and target distributions to learn the transport map with a single, scalable, stable training objective, combined with a damped fixed-point iteration for regularization. On high-dimensional Gaussian mixtures up to d=2500, BMS remains stable and captures all modes, whereas ASBS exhibits performance degradation at these scales, contrasting with prior work typically limited to d=50. title: Flow Matching Calibration for Simulation-Based Inference under Model Misspecification
claim_text: FMCPE refines a simulation-trained posterior estimator using a small set of real calibration samples via two sequential flow-matching stages: a data-space transport map T_X coupling real observations to simulator-space counterparts, and a parameter-space transport map T_Θ moving a simulation-informed source distribution toward the true posterior (Section on method). FMCPE is evaluated on two synthetic benchmarks (a 3-parameter/10-dimensional Gaussian task and a 2-parameter Pendulum task with friction-induced misspecification) and two real-world benchmarks (WindTunnel hatch-angle inference and LightTunnel RGB/polarizer-coefficient inference from 64x64x3 images) (Section on experiments). title: ClinTutor-R1: Advancing Scalable and Robust One-to-Many Alignment in Clinical Socratic Education
claim_text: ClinTutor-R1 achieves an 8.35 average score on MedXpertQA-based clinical Socratic education evaluation, a roughly 20% improvement over its Qwen2.5VL base model score of 6.96 (Table 2). ClinTutor-R1's score of 8.35 is comparable to proprietary reasoning models o3 (8.42) and GPT-4o (8.36) on the same evaluation (Table 2). Ablating components of ClinTutor-R1 shows the RL training stage is most critical: removing RL drops the score to 7.58, removing the thinking stage drops it to 7.94, using a vanilla (non-shaped) reward drops it to 8.01, and removing the veto mechanism drops it to 7.87 with degraded safety behavior (Table 2). As the number of simulated students scales from 1 to 10, ClinTutor-R1 maintains an average score around 8.20, whereas the Med-SocraticLM baseline declines from about 7.5 to below 6.7, a roughly 15% drop (Figure 4, Table 10). title: Disentangling Latent Risk Pathways via Bayesian Hypergraph Inference
claim_text: On UK Biobank data comprising N≈277,291 participants and V=66 chronic disease conditions, BHPI (Bayesian Hypergraph Pathway Inference) is evaluated against per-disease logistic regression and other baselines (Section 5.5, 'UK Biobank: Disentangling Real-World Disease Pathways'). For diseases with prevalence below 2%, BHPI achieves a mean AUC improvement of +1.2 (×100 scale) over per-disease logistic regression, with statistical significance p=3×10^-5 (Table 5). BHPI achieves an expected calibration error of 0.005 on the UK Biobank 66-disease prediction task, below the 0.01 threshold reported as well-calibrated (Table 4, 'Predictive calibration on UKB (66 diseases)'). On simulated data with N=2000, BHPI recovers disease-level risk coefficients with 97.85% correlation to ground truth (cor(β,β̂)) and recovers the true hypergraph structure with 96.96% AUC (H-AUC) (Table 2). title: SceneSmith: Agentic Generation of Simulation-Ready Indoor Scenes
claim_text: SceneSmith generates simulation-ready indoor environments from natural-language prompts through hierarchical stages from architectural layout to furniture and small-object population (Section 3). Each generation stage is implemented as an interaction among VLM agents with designer, critic, and orchestrator roles (Section 3). SceneSmith integrates text-to-3D synthesis for static objects, dataset retrieval for articulated objects, and physical-property estimation (Section 3). Across 210 room- and house-level prompts, SceneSmith generates 3-6x more objects than prior methods, with under 2% inter-object collisions and 96% physics-stable objects (Section 4). In a 205-participant user study, SceneSmith achieves 92.2% average realism and 91.5% prompt-faithfulness win rates against baselines (Table 1). title: Tokenised Flow Matching for Hierarchical Simulation Based Inference
claim_text: Tokenised Flow Matching for Posterior Estimation (TFMPE) uses likelihood-factorisation (LF) sampling that trains a per-site neural surrogate on single simulations and synthesises multi-site observations for posterior training, reducing simulator calls per training sample compared to hierarchical posterior factorisation baselines (Method section on LF sampling). The tokenisation scheme embeds parameters and observations with variable identifiers, intra-variable positions, group identifiers for site membership, and Gaussian Fourier features for functional inputs, processed by an encoder-only transformer producing flow-matching vector fields (Method section on tokenisation and architecture). On a 100-site seasonal SEIR epidemiological model, TFMPE achieves MMD² = 0.060 relative to a NUTS reference (p < 0.005), with NUTS failing to converge beyond 5 sites, and TARP calibration gives ATC = 0.

title: RNA-FM: Flow-Matching Generative Model for Genome-wide RNA-Seq Prediction
claim_text: On TCGA-LUAD with UNI features, RNA-FM achieves a PCC of 0.729 (RMSE 0.074) for the top-1000 genes and PCC of 0.865 (RMSE 0.050) for the top-50 genes (Section 4.2, Table 1). On TCGA-COAD with UNI features, RNA-FM reaches PCC 0.775 for top-1000 genes and PCC 0.943 for top-50 genes, its strongest result among the three TCGA cohorts tested (Section 4.2, Table 1). In external validation on CPTAC, RNA-FM attains top-100 gene PCCs of 0.480 (LUAD), 0.557 (BRCA), and 0.515 (COAD), demonstrating generalization beyond the TCGA training distribution (Section 4.5, Table 3). GO-BP pathway gene predictions outperform GO-MF predictions, with spindle checkpoint signaling pathway PCC improving from 0.623 to 0.682 (Section 4.3, Table 2). title: Hyper-ICL: Attention Calibration with Hyperbolic Anchor Distillation for Multimodal In-Context Learning
claim_text: On Idefics-9b and Idefics2-8B-base, Hyper-ICL (demonstration-free) reaches 62.08/71.17 accuracy on VQAv2, 55.31/62.24 on OK-VQA, and 117.44/135.66 CIDEr on COCO Caption respectively, outperforming learnable baselines LoRA, LIVE, and MimIC while using only 1.18M parameters (Table 1). Hyper-ICL requires only 0.955 TFLOPs at inference, versus 23.364 TFLOPs for standard 32-shot in-context learning, eliminating the need for in-context demonstrations at test time via a low-rank logit-level attention adapter (Section on inference efficiency; Table 1). In held-out transfer experiments (training on one dataset and evaluating on a related task), Hyper-ICL trained on VQAv2 and evaluated on OK-VQA achieves 59.11 accuracy versus 51.43 for standard ICL (Table 8). title: Bridging Time and Frequency: A Joint Modeling Framework for Irregular Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
claim_text: TFMixer introduces a learnable Non-Uniform Discrete Fourier Transform (NUDFT) that extracts spectral representations directly from irregular timestamps without requiring interpolation, used in its Global Frequency Module with spectral refinement via an MLP and an inverse NUDFT to produce a seasonal bias (Abstract, Section 4.2). TFMixer's Local Time Module uses transformable patch encoding with continuous time embeddings and a query-based patch attention mechanism designed to address information density imbalance across non-uniform patches, combined with dual-mixing blocks for temporal and cross-variable dependencies (Section 4.3). On irregular multivariate time series forecasting benchmarks (PhysioNet, MIMIC, HumanActivity, USHCN), TFMixer achieves a 3.0% MSE reduction and 8.1% MAE reduction versus the second-best baseline, APN (Table 1, Section A.1). title: SEER: Transformer-based Robust Time Series Forecasting via Automated Patch Enhancement and Replacement
claim_text: SEER's Learnable Patch Replacement Module operates in two stages: an Automated Token Filter (Section 4.3.1) that produces sigmoid-based quality scores to filter tokens below a threshold, preserving gradient flow via detachment tricks (Equations 9-11), followed by Replaced Causal Self-Attention (Section 4.3.2) that substitutes filtered low-quality patches with series-wise prototype tokens before applying causally-masked multi-head self-attention (Equations 12-14). Across 8 multivariate forecasting benchmark datasets and forecast horizons {96, 192, 336, 720}, SEER ranks first in 34 of 45 MSE settings and 39 of 45 MAE settings, yielding an average 7.3% MSE reduction and 4.9% MAE reduction over the second-best baseline, xPatch (Table 2). title: PyHealth 2.0: A Comprehensive Open-Source Toolkit for Accessible and Reproducible Clinical Deep Learning
claim_text: PyHealth 2.0 unifies 15+ datasets, 20+ clinical tasks, 25+ models, and 5+ interpretability methods (Attention-Grad, GIM, DeepLift, SHAP among them) spanning EHR, imaging, physiological signal, and genomic modalities (Section 3; Appendices F-J). On MIMIC-IV in-hospital mortality prediction, PyHealth 2.0 with 16 workers processes data in 2,385 seconds versus 93,708 seconds for a naive pandas implementation, a roughly 39x speedup, while reducing peak memory from 146.23-457.42 GB (PyHealth 1.16) to 17.48-28.70 GB, about a 20x reduction (Table 3). On drug recommendation and length-of-stay prediction tasks, PyHealth 2.0 still yields substantial speedups over pandas (4,725s to 569s, and 10,269s to 1,096s respectively), though smaller than the 39x mortality-prediction speedup (Tables 4 and 5). title: SCRWKV: Ultra-Compact Structure-Calibrated Vision-RWKV for Topological Crack Segmentation
claim_text: SCRWKV, built around a Structure-Field Encoder (SFE) backbone, uses only 1.22M parameters and 22.78G FLOPs (28MB model size) while achieving F1=0.9363/mIoU=0.9289 on DeepCrack and F1=0.8428/mIoU=0.8512 on TUT (Table 1, Table 2). SCRWKV outperforms 10 prior SOTA crack-segmentation methods across all four benchmark datasets (Crack500, DeepCrack, CrackMap, TUT) despite its far smaller parameter count (Table 1). Geometry-guided Bidirectional Structure Transformation (GBST) models curvilinear crack manifolds via counter-directional streams and is shown in component ablations to outperform alternative interaction mechanisms such as bi_ParaSnake, DiagSnake, and Q-Shift (Figure 3, Table 5). Dynamic Self-Calibrating Decay (DSCD) is shown via ablation, alongside AMCM and GBST, to be a necessary component contributing to overall segmentation accuracy on the benchmark datasets (Table 3). title: Exploring Accurate and Transparent Domain Adaptation in Predictive Healthcare via Concept-Grounded Orthogonal Inference
claim_text: ExtraCare improves weighted-F1 diagnosis prediction on eICU from a base of 61.09% to 68.61%, and heart-failure prediction F1 from 72.76% to 79.64%, under spatial domain shift (Table 2, Section 4.2). On the OCHIN dataset under temporal domain shift, ExtraCare raises diagnosis weighted-F1 from 63.77% to 74.05% and heart-failure F1 from 74.88% to 85.38% (Table 2, Section 4.2).
